/journal/johnsons-circle/.description: The bookseller Joseph Johnson (1738–1809) of 72 St Paul's Churchyard was Blake's principal commercial employer from c. 1779 onward. Johnson commissioned the Original Stories engravings after Wollstonecraft (1791), the Stedman Narrative plates (1791–96), and set Blake's The French Revolution (1791) in type. Johnson's weekly Tuesday dinners brought together radical writers, scientists, and artists — Thomas Paine, Joseph Priestley, William Godwin, Mary Wollstonecraft, Henry Fuseli, and Blake.
/journal/johnsons-circle/.preview: Joseph Johnson opened his bookshop at 72 St Paul's Churchyard, London, in 1761 and rapidly became the principal commercial patron of dissenting and radical writers in late-Georgian England. Knowles records Sir Andrew Hamilton's introduction of Fuseli to Johnson c. 1764:
/journal/johnsons-circle/.title: Joseph Johnson's Circle, St Paul's Churchyard

/journal/lambeth/.preview: Blake and Catherine moved from 28 Poland Street, Soho, to No. 13 Hercules Buildings, Lambeth, in late 1790. /journal/linnell-on-tatham/.title: Linnell on Tatham's Disposal of Blake's Manuscripts

/letters/1808-12-19-to-cumberland/.description: From South Molton Street; thanks for Cumberland's encouragement.
/letters/1808-12-19-to-cumberland/.title: To Cumberland

/letters/1818-06-09-to-dawson-turner/.description: Blake's own catalogue raisonné of the illuminated books with prices. Essential as a primary-source price-list.
/letters/1818-06-09-to-dawson-turner/.title: To Dawson Turner — 9 June 1818

/letters/1819-10-04-to-linnell-first/.description: First extant letter to Linnell. Bridges the long 1818-1825 silence.
/letters/1819-10-04-to-linnell-first/.title: To Linnell

/letters/1825-10-11-to-linnell/.description: On accompanying Linnell partway by coach; among the earliest of the deathbed-period letters.
/letters/1825-10-11-to-linnell/.title: To Linnell

/letters/1825-11-10-to-linnell/.description: First explicit mention of the Job plates in the Linnell correspondence — 'the plates would be all the better for it.' Bridges 1825-10-11 and 1826-02-01.
/letters/1825-11-10-to-linnell/.title: To Linnell

/letters/1826-02-01-to-linnell/.description: Too ill to come; invites Linnell to share a mutton chop instead.
/letters/1826-02-01-to-linnell/.title: To Linnell

/letters/1826-07-29-to-linnell/.description: On Dr Young's prescription (dandelion addition); delirium and pain too sharp for thought.
/letters/1826-07-29-to-linnell/.title: To Linnell

/letters/1826-08-01-to-linnell/.description: Mid-illness summer letter; 'only bones and sinews, all strings and bobbins like a weaver's loom.'
/letters/1826-08-01-to-linnell/.title: To Linnell

/letters/1827-04-25-to-linnell/.description: Recovery in progress; thanks for £10; on Job, Dante engravings, the Stedman plates.
/letters/1827-04-25-to-linnell/.title: To Linnell

/letters/1827-07-03-to-linnell/.description: Final Linnell letter; relapse after Hampstead; thanks for £10. Blake dies six weeks later.
/letters/1827-07-03-to-linnell/.title: To Linnell

/other-writings/.description: Manuscripts, drafts, and prose works that Blake wrote but did not engrave. Source texts are public-domain editions (Ellis-Yeats 1893, Gilchrist 1880, Sampson 1905) transcribed verbatim with citation.
/other-writings/.title: Other Writings

/other-writings/notes-in-other-men-s-boo.description: Marginal notes Blake wrote in another author's published book. Edmond Malone (1798).

/other-writings/notes-in-other-men-s-boo.description: Blake's marginal annotations in his own copy of The Works of Sir Joshua Reynolds, ed. Edmond Malone (3 vols., 1798). Public-domain transcription from Ellis & Yeats (1893).

/other-writings/the-notebook/.description: Selections from Blake's Notebook (Rossetti Manuscript), now British Library Add. MS 49460. Blake used the notebook from c. 1787 (after his brother Robert's death) through to his old age.
/other-writings/the-notebook/.title: The Notebook

/other-writings/the-notebook/everlasting.description: A long verse fragment from Blake's Notebook (Rossetti Manuscript), c. 1818. Public-domain text below extracted from Ellis & Yeats (1893).
/other-writings/the-notebook/everlasting.preview: A long verse fragment drafted by Blake in the Notebook (Rossetti Manuscript, now BL Add. MS 49460) in the years after the 1809 Exhibition, datable to c. 1818. Never engraved. The text contests the orthodox image of Christ as meek and submissive, asserting an alternative vision.
/other-writings/the-notebook/everlasting.title: The Everlasting Gospel

/other-writings/the-notebook/vision-of-t.description: Blake's prose meditation on his own painting A Last Judgment (now lost), drafted in the Notebook c. 1810. Survives as the principal late prose statement of Blake's aesthetic theory.
